title: The Diabolical Envy and the Human Mind
english: It is appropriate for anyone who intends to conduct an examination of a certain discourse to take the premises of the discourse into account, in what is now being composed, and especially since the presented book, being most useful, does not have an unapproachable intellect. For within it, the whole discourse concerning the judgments of God is moved by Job, and how nothing of the things happening occurs to men except by the concurrence of God (Job 29:22), and other dogmatic theorems—and even in the preceding discourse, things concerning patience and endurance and the attitudes of the indifferent—I say, goods and possessions and many children and good upbringing—to these are added the manifestation of free will and the teaching of various dogmas, as we see God giving them according to each of the matters, into which these things are. If, therefore, the premise is necessary, it is sufficient.

A change in the value of things appears to be a variation, this being of bodies decaying and increasing, and this being of a change occurring through choice. And as many as occur according to the body, they show neither an unseemly underlying substance nor a praiseworthy one. For no one is acceptable either in the decay of the body or in its increase; for these things are outside of what is up to us. But as many as are done by the one acting while the reasoning is moving volitionally, these show him either rejected or praiseworthy. And this follows those who change from wickedness to virtue or from virtue to wickedness.

So it has happened that a rational being became an apostate from God, 'having made a neck [bowed] before the Lord of all' (Job 29:22). And this is the devil, not having become a devil—for 'God did not make death' (Wisdom 1:13)—but perfect and virtuous—for 'God made all things very good' (Gen 1:31)—who, having fallen from the right state and blessedness, envies those turning toward this; for 'through the envy of the devil, death entered into the world' (Wisdom 2:24). For he reasons as an outcast toward himself that: it is necessary to obstruct the heavenly...

They are a polity, so that those whom I fell from might ascend. For he thinks the progress of men to be a private accusation, because he himself is the 'Morning Star' of the heavens and a star 'rising at dawn' that shines, but because he was preparing those who would be enlightened by the 'Sun of Righteousness' [Mal 4:2], he fell from the heavenly regions. But these, as I see, hasten toward the visible polity, who have more inclination toward wickedness.

For 'carefully the mind of men is set upon evil things' [1 Cor 6:3], which the apostle wishes to demonstrate, saying: 'Shall we judge angels?' [1 Cor 6:3]; meaning that we, living the heavenly life upon earth, judge those who do not guard their own order, just as the Ninevites judge the Jews for not having believed in the Savior, themselves having been persuaded by the preaching of Jonah concerning repentance. But also that which is said concerning the Queen of Sheba [Matt 12:42] is a demonstration of the same mind; for a woman and a queen, standing far off and intending to travel through foreign districts, having surpassed all these things of Solomon's wisdom, she hastened to be obedient, the Jews having the teacher as a pledge and not wishing to be benefited by him, even though Solomon had more. For he was benefited having been instructed by him, but the Savior was shown to be a wonder-worker capable of persuading the most unbelieving ones by the benefit from the words and signs and wonders; for resurrections of the dead, openings of eyes to the blind, cleansings of lepers, and in general a healing of 'every disease and infirmity' [Matt 9:35] was performed by him.

This, then, was the diabolical envy, because men were hastening to lay hold of those things from which he himself fell. Therefore also he does not neglect the influence against the race; for our 'adversary the devil walks like a lion seeking someone to devour' [1 Pet 5:8]. In this way also, having cast a calculation of love of silver into Judah, he made him a traitor to the Savior, just as into a household.
